idiom_name: struct with unexported fields and methods, all in one package
implementation_notes: Go's boundaries are packages and the compiler enforces them: a method can only be declared in the package that declares the type, unexported (lowercase) fields and functions are invisible to importers, and an import cycle that would smuggle one part of the model into another is a compile error. A standalone type is therefore a plain struct with unexported fields, a constructor (`New...`) that validates and small exported methods - the classic private-members structure has nothing left to hand-write, and the exported surface is itself the class's complete definition. Keep that surface small (the Go blog's 'minimize the exported interface') and prefer defining small interfaces at the consumer instead of importing model types; the proverb 'a little copying is better than a little dependency' states this pattern directly.
pitfalls: An exported struct with exported fields is writable by every importer: invariants then hold only by convention and the zero value may be invalid - keep fields unexported and give the zero value a defined meaning.
Embedding a struct from another package promotes its methods and re-imports its meaning; anonymous embedding is composition, not a way to stay standalone.
Interface satisfaction is implicit, so a standalone type that happens to match a large consumer interface is coupled to it anyway; keep interfaces small and declare them where they are used.
Unexported helpers are visible to the whole package, not to the type: in a big package the 'private method' boundary is the package, so keep packages small and named after the concept.
